Upbringing makes a person humane by forming them inside relationships and their rituals, and a model rewarded for outputs stands in no relationship it could owe anything to. Book 13's concern with correct names applies directly. If we call a tuned model good, the word will slide from describing a person formed in relationships to describing a product that passes evaluation, and people will start judging each other by the second sense.

Humaneness is realised between people who can hold one another to account. A model can be adjusted when it errs, but it cannot be reproached, forgiven or trusted in the way a person raised well can, so whatever it has is not goodness in that sense. A company says its assistant has been raised with good values. The assistant has no parent, no teacher and no one it owes anything to; it has a reward signal.

An Ubuntu Ethicist will object that the Confucian ties goodness to fixed roles, when a person becomes good through relationships of solidarity that need not follow any hierarchy of roles. Relationships of solidarity are not opposed to roles; they are carried in them, as friend, neighbour, colleague. Either way the point stands: the model enters no relationships at all, so neither account makes it good. A child is raised into a household's ways over years; the model is raised into nothing, only scored.

Training can make a model behave acceptably, but moral upbringing makes a person someone who owes and is owed, and no feedback signal does that. A child is raised inside roles: as a son or daughter, a pupil, a younger sibling. What they learn is not a list of approved acts but how to be each of these to particular people, and the learning happens through the relationships themselves.

Book 13's concern with correct names applies directly. If we call a tuned model good, the word will slide from describing a person formed in relationships to describing a product that passes evaluation, and people will start judging each other by the second sense.

A Utilitarian will object that what makes behaviour good is what it does to people, so a model that reliably helps and does not harm is good in the only sense that matters, whatever its upbringing. Helpful outputs are good to have, but the motion claims more: that the model is good the way a well-raised person is. That sense includes standing in relationships where one can be held to account, and an output profile does not supply it. A model may learn to say the right words, but it has no role in which to practise them and no elder or child to practise them for.

I reject the motion. Calling a trained model good in the sense a well-raised child is good is a name that does not fit the thing, and the misnaming has consequences. Ritual propriety is learned by taking part in shared forms of conduct with others who also take part. A model that is scored on its replies takes part in nothing; it is shaped from outside by raters it does not stand in any relation to.
